extracted.intended_audience: legislators, electoral reformers, political theorists, and informed citizens interested in designing fair parliamentary elections
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidelines and practical standards for structuring parliamentary elections: mode of voting (public vs secret), nomination and campaign finance rules, polling logistics, candidate remuneration, and term length to balance responsibility and latitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct election over indirect
rubrics_metrics.description: Every benefit of indirect election which is attainable at all is attainable under direct; indirect election is an additional and superfluous wheel, decidedly inferior as a means of cultivating public spirit and political intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect election reduces voter identification with their representative and the member's sense of responsibility, concentrates power in a small number of electors (increasing opportunities for intrigue and corruption), and tends to reduce constituencies to conditions favorable for bribery. Exception: circumstances similar to the election of U.S. senators (i.e., special institutional contexts) may justify indirect methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public voting (publicity) is generally preferable to secret ballot
rubrics_metrics.description: In political elections the cases where secret voting is preferable are the exception, not the rule; the spirit of the ballot tends to suggest that suffrage is for the voter's private use rather than a public trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicity promotes the sense that the vote is a trust and makes voters answerable to the public, encouraging honesty, deliberation, and restraint. Secret voting risks encouraging votes given for private or class interest, selfishness, or mere caprice. The moral effect and public impression of the institution are crucial in its operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow secret ballot only in exceptional circumstances of coercion or oligarchic domination
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest case for the ballot is when the mischievous power of the Few over the Many is increasing; historically (e.g., decline of Roman republic, some Athenian cases) the ballot protected voters from coercion and intimidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use secret voting to defend the franchise where coercion, intimidation, or bribery by powerful actors is prevalent and where publicity would entrench oligarchic control. But in modern contexts where coercive influence is declining, secrecy may do more harm by removing public restraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the vote as a public trust, not merely a private right
rubrics_metrics.description: The suffrage is morally a trust; the voter is bound to give his vote according to his best and most conscientious opinion of the public good, not for personal advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If voters regard the franchise as a private right, they may sell or misuse it. Institutions should cultivate the understanding that voting is a duty toward the public, and design procedures (such as publicity) that signal and reinforce that moral obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require signature and public validation for voting papers (no unmonitored postal/home voting)
rubrics_metrics.description: If voting papers are used, the signature of the elector should be affixed to the paper at a public polling-place, or at an office open to all, in the presence of a responsible public officer; allowing papers to be filled at home or sent by post is fatal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal or home completion enables bribers and intimidators to monitor or enforce bargains in privacy and removes salutary public influences. Even when employing systems (e.g., Hare's personal representation) that necessitate ballots/papers, ensure public authentication to preserve accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polling places must be numerous, accessible, and publicly funded
rubrics_metrics.description: Polling places should be so numerous as to be within easy reach of every voter; hustings, poll clerks, and all necessary machinery of elections should be at the public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No expenses of conveyance at the cost of the candidate should be tolerated; the state/locality may provide conveyance only for the infirm on medical certificate. Public funding of logistics prevents candidates from using resources to skew access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit candidate-funded conveyance and limit candidate election expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: No expenses of conveyance at the cost of the candidate should be tolerated under any pretext; the candidate should not be permitted to incur any but a limited and trifling expense for his election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent candidates buying votes or access via paid transport. Limit the candidate's direct expenses to protect against elections becoming an auction for wealth and to reduce barriers to entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require a modest deposit to deter frivolous candidates, with limited allowable use
rubrics_metrics.description: A sum (proposed L50, possibly L100) should be required from every one who places his name on the list of candidates to prevent persons without real intention or chance from becoming candidates; the deposit may be used for necessary advertising (advertisements, placards, circulars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposit discourages wanton candidacies that split needed votes. Allow limited use for necessary campaign disclosure but make expenses beyond deposit illegal and punishable to curb excessive spending. Supporters' voluntary expenses cannot be fully prevented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require post-election declaration on expenses and penalize falsehood (perjury)
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration on oath or honor should be required from every member, on taking his seat, that he had not expended, nor would expend, money or money's worth beyond the allowed deposit for the purposes of his election; falsehood should be punishable as perjury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal penalties and public seriousness about enforcement would shift opinion and reduce tolerance for electoral corruption. 'Opinion tolerates a false disclaimer only when it already tolerates the thing disclaimed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage payment for seats and the commercialization of elective office
rubrics_metrics.description: So long as the elected member, in any shape or manner, pays for his seat, all endeavours will fail to make the business of election anything but a selfish bargain on all sides; political functions should not be represented as a favor to be bought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid practices that present office as pecuniary advantage; creating the impression that members seek seats for personal gain undermines voters' sense of duty and public spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: If remuneration is necessary, provide indemnity for loss, not a salary
rubrics_metrics.description: If payment is needed so that fit persons without independent means can serve, the payment should be an indemnity for loss of time or money, not a salary; a salary would make the occupation a profession and attract adventurers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remuneration should remove undue financial barriers without converting parliamentary service into a paid profession whose primary motive is pecuniary. Exceptional cases may be served by public subscription to support a particularly qualified but impecunious individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit candidate advertising and make excessive campaign spending illegal and punishable
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary expenses for making claims known (advertisements, placards, circulars) should be allowable within the deposit; any expenses beyond that (out of the candidate's pocket) should be illegal and punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep campaigning costs limited to prevent wealth from determining access; combined with deposit and declarations, this aims to change norms that tolerate costly elections as a conservative filter for class exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance parliamentary term length to preserve responsibility and allow demonstration of merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should not have so long a tenure as to forget responsibility or neglect conferences with constituents, nor so short a term that they can only be judged by a single act; term length must allow time to show qualities yet maintain popular control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where democratic power is weak or representatives enter aristocratic atmospheres, more frequent returns are necessary. No universal rule—application depends on constitutional context and strength of democratic institutions.
